about: What NuclearLang, Synapsis and their tools can do today, by area. Each row names the kinds and commands that do it.

rows.title: Can: an HTTP API with validation (backend)
rows.summary: A backend exposes REST routes with controllers (`@get`, `@post`, `@put`, `@patch`, `@delete`), reads and answers validated models, turns a `Result` error into its HTTP status, checks guards on its routes, serves the same routes over a WebSocket when configured, and publishes its contract and OpenAPI document.
body: - `@controller("books") controller BooksController(books: BooksAppComponent)` with one method per route; `{id}` in a route is a path parameter, a model parameter is the JSON body.

- Models validate the input with rule decorators (`@required`, `@minLength`, `@maxLength`, `@min`, `@max`, `@pattern`, `@email`, `@url`); an invalid body is a 400 with the reasons (every dialect). A value of another JSON type is refused (rule `type`): `"30"` is not an `int`, `1` is not a `bool`, a number is not a `string` nor a `DateTime`; `30.0` is an `int` and a whole number is a `double`; a path or query parameter is text and is converted. A model built in code (`NewTask(title = "")`) is checked too and throws.

- An `Err(NotFound(...))` answers 404; `Invalid` 400, `Unauthorized` 401, `Forbidden` 403, `Conflict` 409. A `@post` answers 201; `status = 200` in the decorator changes it. What the database refuses for integrity (a repeated unique value that two requests sent at once) answers 409 `conflict`, never a 500.
- Guards: `guards: Guard[] = [NoOrigin(), Token(value = env("TOKEN"))]` in the `appConfig`, `@controller("x", guards = [...])` for one controller (see can:backend-guards).
- `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` in the connections serves the same controllers over a WebSocket (see can:real-time).
- The build serves `/.nuclear/contract.json` and `/.nuclear/openapi.json`.
- The same Nuclear builds as a Python service (`fastapi`) or a TypeScript one (`nestjs`).

rows.title: Can: a database with entities, relations, queries, transactions and migrations (backend)
rows.summary: A backend stores data with entities (tables), repositories (CRUD and queries built line by line), relations between entities, pages, transactions and migrations, on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB.
body: - `entity` with `@primary(generated = true)`, `@column(length, unique, index, nullable, default, name)`, `@created`, `@updated`. A `string` without `length` holds 255 characters; a long text is a larger `length` (`@column(length = 100000)`): where the database's `VARCHAR` cannot hold it the column is its text type, the same in every dialect; there is no other word. A `DateTime` column keeps its fraction of a second on every database.
- Relations: `@manyToOne` (with its column `<name>Id`), `@oneToMany`, `@manyToMany` + `@joinTable`, `@oneToOne` + `@joinColumn`; loaded with `relations("tasks")`.

- `repository`: `find`, `findAll`, `save`, `remove` come with it; a method's lines build one query: `where({...})` with `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `ne`, `like`, `ilike`, `oneOf`, `isNull`, `between`; `orderBy`, `limit`, `offset`; then `getOne()`, `getMany()`, `paginate(page, size)`, `count()`, `exists()`, `update({...})`, `delete()`. `like` follows the database's rule for upper and lower case; `ilike` is the same on every database.
- `@transactional` on a use case's `exec`: one transaction; an `Err` rolls it back.

- Migrations, the same in every dialect (TypeORM's behaviour is their rule): `nuclear migrate make "<message>"`, `nuclear migrate [--to <migration>]`, `nuclear migrate down [--to <migration>]`, `nuclear migrate status`; `--fake` marks them applied or reverted without running them (a database that already has the tables), `--transaction all|each|none` (default `all`). A renamed table or column is told to `make`, or its data is dropped: `nuclear migrate make "<message>" --rename shops=stores --rename orders.shop_id=store_id` (the database's names).
- Plugins: `sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`. Tests run on an in-memory database. `createTables = true` (development) makes the same schema the migrations make.
Both dialects are checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB 11 in Docker (`platforms/backend/checks/database-check`): the same answers, byte for byte.

rows.title: Can: call another HTTP API (every platform)
rows.summary: A repository whose methods carry `@get`, `@post`, `@put`, `@patch` or `@delete` and no body calls the `Http(baseUrl)` connection: path parameters, the query or the body are filled from the method's parameters, and an error status is the `Err` of its `Result`.
body: ```nuclear
@repository(path = "character")
repository CharacterRepository
@get(path = ":id")
one(id: int) Result<Error, Character>
- `:id` takes the parameter `id`; the other parameters go to the query (GET) or the body.
- The connection is `Http(baseUrl = "https://...")` in `appConfig`.
- A JSON key that is not the field's name gets `@key("air_date")` on the model's field.
- On mobile and web, `cache`, `ttl` and `retry` are options of the request; on mobile, `saveLocal = true` keeps the answers in the device's database.
- `nuclear gen resource ... --from-json <url>` writes the whole resource from the API's own answer.

rows.title: Can: events, a cache and AI agents (backend)
rows.summary: A backend publishes and consumes events (in the process or through Kafka), caches with Redis, and declares AI agents: tools, agents with memory per thread and graphs of steps, on Ollama or OpenAI models, with a vector store.
body: - Events: `~publish("topic", value)`; `listener Name` with `@consumer("topic")` methods; the clients of the app's WebSocket subscribed to the topic receive it too. Plugins `events`, `kafka`, `websocket`.
- Cache: the `redis` plugin.

- AI (plugin `ai`, with `ollama` or `openai`): `tools Name` (each method with a doc comment is a tool), `agent Name(tools: T)` with a `prompt`, `@state(S) graph Name` whose methods are nodes (`@start`, `@next("node")`), a `state` for the graph, `Chroma` vectors (plugin `chroma`).
- A test replaces the model with `FakeModel(["answer"])`.
The Nuclear Developer (NuclearLang's local agents, on standby) is itself written with these kinds.

rows.title: Can: a mobile app (mobile)
rows.summary: A mobile app with screens and navigation, state managers, forms with validation, translations, a session with roles and guards, events, HTTP repositories with cache, an encrypted local database, and AI chats and flows; it runs on Android, iOS, desktop and web.
body: - Views: `stateless` and `stateful` with the UI toolkit's classes; `@screen(route, providers, acl, transition)`; navigation by screen (`context.goTo`, `pushTo`, `goBack`).
- State: `statemanager` + state model, `<State>Builder` in the view.
- Forms: a form model with rules, a `formmanager`, `SynapsisForm` in the view.
- Texts: `"component.screen.key".tr()` from `assets/i18n/<locale>/<component>.json`.
- Session and access: `SessionManager`, `guard`, `@acl(roles = [...])`, `@screen(acl = {...})`.
- Events: `event`, `Events.publish`, `@on(Event)`.
- Data: HTTP repositories (`cache`, `ttl`, `retry`), and a local database: `@primary` on a model gives it an encrypted table, `saveLocal = true` keeps what a GET answers.
- AI (plugin `genkit`): `tools`, `chat`, `flow`, `remote`, `knowledge`.
- Tests: `@mock`, `@test`, `@states`, `@widget`, integration tests.
- Run and debug: `nuclear run`, `nuclear device` (a test device in its own window), breakpoints on `.nuc` lines in VS Code.

rows.title: Can: a web app (web)
rows.summary: A web app with screens and routing, views as HTML functions, state managers, repositories over HTTP or a WebSocket (with what the server pushes), use cases, events, guards and tests; it also mounts in a host's page. The words are the mobile platform's.
body: - Views: `stateless` and `stateful` with `build() Element` and HTML functions (`main`, `ul`, `li`, `button`) with named attributes and `children`. No JSX.
- `@screen(route, providers, acl, notFound)`; navigation by screen: `goTo(Screen, id = 7)`, `goBack()`.
- `statemanager` + state model, `<State>Builder` with one callback per state.

- `repository` over HTTP (`cache`, `ttl`, `retry`) or over a `WebSocket` connection with the same methods; `@on("topic")` methods return `Stream<T>` of what the server pushes; `usecase`, `appcomponent`, `service`, `event`, `guard`.
- Tests: `@mock`, `@test`, `@states`, `@widget` with `renderScreen`.
- `mount(element, host)`: the same app in a host's page (see can:web-embedded).
- `nuclear new <name> -p web`, `nuclear build | install | run | test`.
The NuclearLang website is written with it.

rows.title: Can: generate the finished code of a resource from its data
rows.summary: `nuclear gen resource` writes, on any platform, the models, the repository, a use case per action, the facade, the controller or the screen and the tests of a resource, all compiling; the fields come from a list, from an example answer of an API (a file or a URL) or from a spec.
body: - `--fields "id:int name:string origin:Origin?"`, `--from-json <file|url>` (nested objects become models, a list under `results` a page, `null` an optional field) or `--from-spec <spec.md>` (its example answer, its `Key | Type` table, its `GET <url>` line).
- `--source rest[:<base url>]` (an API) or `--source db` (an entity and its queries, backend only).
- `--actions list,get,search,create,update,delete`; `--screen <screen>` on mobile and web; `--dry-run` shows the files.
- It refuses, before writing, a field type nobody declared, a name another file declares and a source the platform has no pieces for. Nothing is overwritten.

- `nuclear gen usecase <component> <Name>` wires a use case the project declares: its alias in the facade and, on the backend, `--route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"` adds its route to the controller of `orders` (made when missing). With `--calls <Repository>.<method>` it also writes the use case, when all it does is call that method.
- `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` writes the smallest file of any kind of the platform.
- The same generators are MCP tools and the first stage of the Builder.

rows.title: Can: build the same project with another dialect of its platform
rows.summary: A backend written once builds as FastAPI (Python) or as NestJS (TypeScript): change `dialect` in `config.nuc` and build. No other file changes, because kinds, decorators, the library and the tests belong to the platform.
body: ```nuclear
synapsis(platform = "backend", dialect = "nestjs")   // was "fastapi"
Then `nuclear build && nuclear install && nuclear test`. The example `tasks_api` is built and tested with both.
The exception: code that uses a library of one target through its type definitions is tied to that target's dialect. Mobile and web have one dialect each today.

rows.title: Can: check a project, apply the exact fixes and format it
rows.summary: `nuclear check` reports every error of a file or a project with its code, place and fix (JSON for agents); `nuclear fix` applies the exact fixes; `nuclear fmt` rewrites the layout; `nuclear explain` tells a run-time error or a failing test at its `.nuc` lines.
body: - `nuclear check . --json`: syntax, names, results, the library, the kinds' rules and the project's architecture, all at once. It also writes the project map (`.nuclear/map.md`).
- `nuclear fix <folder|file>`: applies every exact fix, then reports what is left.
- `nuclear fmt <file|folder> [--check]`: spacing, indentation and blank lines; it never reorders.
- `nuclear explain`: reads a stack or a test's output and answers the message, a hint and the `.nuc` lines.
- `nuclear repair` (mobile): rebuilds from scratch until the target's analyzer finds no errors.
- `nuclear doctor`: what the machine lacks.

rows.title: Can: take a spec to tested code with AI agents, on your machine or under a frontier model
rows.summary: The Builder runs a spec through the factory's stations with a team (each role done by a provider's agent or a provider's model); every run is documented, waits at its gates for you, and is exportable as CI.
body: - From a terminal: `nuclear-builder run specs/<component>/<id>/spec.md` runs the factory (Analysis, Design, Tests first, Code, Quality, Delivery) with the run's team (`nuclear-builder team …`); `--lead` is ignored. Or ask a team's tech lead in Nuclear Chat: it writes the spec and starts the run (in a workspace, in the app the spec is for).
- The editors run the same factory as a process: VS Code's Builder page and Android Studio's tool window (the team, the gates, QA's checks, the two spending questions).

- VS Code's Builder opens a run on its progress: the stations in a line with who works each, what is done now or what waits for your answer, and the spec it works on with its criteria (*Technical diagram* for the detailed one); a run the team starts from the chat appears there by itself.

- Nuclear Chat under the Builder's diagram (and as a full tab): each run is a thread of its team's channel, told by the member of each station, its gates and QA's plan as buttons that answer the run; a member does everything the page does (`nuclear-builder mcp`, see can:agents-do-everything): reads the slides, writes specs with their criteria (`spec_new`), starts runs, answers gates, or proposes a change of a spec as a difference the user accepts (`nuclear-builder spec accept|discard`); anything a paid member spends is confirmed twice in the editor.

- The teams as your software company (VS Code): each team any number of members per role, hired with a wizard (a suggested name, the purpose and skills, members suggested with why, the roster's filters, who works each member and what it costs: `nuclear-builder team create|suggest|name-suggest|member add`), a logo, a description and a tech lead who answers for it; a run's node reads like a debugger, and who did each step is one label, `<employee> · <role> · <provider> · <model>`.
- Specs imported from Jira or a GitHub issue (VS Code).
- The internet for facts: `web_search`, `web_read`, `api_inspect` (MCP tools).
- CI: `nuclear-builder export github|gitlab|bitbucket`; `nuclear-builder ci` runs the same commands locally.

- A direct message with the general agent (Atlas, `nuclear-builder member --role chat`, its provider in `nuclear.builder.chat`): Nuclear Atlas's page (VS Code); it informs and runs no task: `/task` there is answered with the tech leads to ask.

rows.title: Can: work with your factory's teams in a chat, as a company works in Slack (Nuclear Chat)
rows.summary: Nuclear Chat is the factory's workplace: channels, direct messages, threads, mentions, reactions and GIFs, local to the project (`.nuclear/chat/`). A member answers as themselves through their provider; a message to a team is answered by its tech lead; a member that does not understand asks. A local service on `127.0.0.1:7880`, every route guarded by a token kept in the keyring (a `0600` file without one).
body: - A host (the Builder, Nuclear Atlas) registers a project with its members, teams and channels: `POST workspaces`; a host gets the URL and the token from `nuclear-chat connect --json` (header `X-Chat-Token`; a request with an `Origin` is refused).

- In VS Code the Builder and Nuclear Atlas are its hosts: the dock under the Builder's diagram and the tab (*Open the chat*) on the team's channel, Atlas on `dm-atlas` or the conversation it was on last in that folder; in the Nuclear workspace Atlas's channels and direct messages fill the column (the page's `?part=sidebar`) beside the page, which shows only the open conversation (`?part=channel`), each following the other; one WebSocket per window holds the token (a page never does), each member's face drawn, `nuclear.chat.gifs` (`pack`, `tenor`, `giphy`) passed as the workspace's GIFs and the key kept with *Nuclear Chat: Keep a GIF Service's Key*.
- A run of the factory is a thread of its team's channel; `/poc <what>` is not available yet (the factory cannot run on a scratch folder).

- Who answers: a direct message's member; `@<member>` by id, name, first name or role; `@<team>`, or a team's channel without a member mentioned: the team's tech lead; the folder's own channel (named after the workspace or the project, `home`) is the team assigned to that folder or its workspace: its tech lead answers there.

- A member answers through its responder, a command run once per answer with `--events` (the conversation in, `typing`, `text`, `tool`, `ask`, `done` out); its questions reach the user and the answer goes back to it; the cost is shown on the message.

- A front for any agent: a direct message with the general agent (Atlas) has a menu in its header to choose who answers it, as in Claude's own app: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build or an API model, each with its model; by default the first agent installed, else an API provider with a key, else it says a provider must be chosen; only what is on this machine is offered (`nuclear-builder agents --json`, the MCP tool `agents_list`; one not found disabled with why). The choice is kept per conversation (`PUT channels/{ws}/{channel}/agent`, `channels.json`); the setting `nuclear.builder.chat` is the default for new ones; a paid agent is still confirmed twice. The answer arrives as it is written (`text-delta` → the event `message.delta`; Claude Code streams), with its markdown, code, tool chips and cost.

- A member answers in the user's chosen language (`nuclear.language`), or in the language the user wrote in; may end an answer with a GIF of the pack by personality; a direct message shows under the member's name the brain that answers (`<agent> · <model> · paid|local`).
- The history is append-only JSON lines per channel (edits and reactions are lines, a crash loses nothing), searchable, with unread counts.
- Real time: the service's WebSocket (`/ws`) serves the same routes and pushes each workspace's events (`{"subscribe": "chat.<workspace>"}`); `GET events/{ws}?since=` reads what a client missed.

- GIFs: a pack of 36 animated drawings made for the project (works offline); a member sends one by personality; Tenor or Giphy only with a key in the keyring (`nuclear-chat gif-key tenor`) and the project's yes, asked once.
- Started at login by the AI set-up (`nuclear-builder setup`); by hand: `nuclear-chat serve`.

- Conversations as in Slack, each a route a host or an agent calls too: edit the user's message (`PATCH messages/{ws}/message/{id}`), delete any (`DELETE`, it shows deleted, its thread stays); close, archive, open again, rename or retopic a conversation (`PATCH channels/{ws}/{channel}` `{state|name|topic}`), delete it (`DELETE channels/{ws}/{channel}`: its history moved to `.nuclear/chat/deleted/`); make a channel with chosen members (`POST channels/{ws}`). In the page: *New message* and Ctrl+K open the quick switcher (any member's direct message, any channel), *Members* lists everyone, the header's ⋯ holds the conversation's actions.

- Search every message: `GET messages/{ws}/search?words=` with `from:@<member>` (`from:@you`) and `in:#<channel>`; in the page the header's *Search*, whose result opens the message highlighted in its channel or thread; a host opens the page at a message with `/<ws>/<channel>?message=<id>&thread=<id>` (VS Code's chat notifications do).

- Who is listed: Atlas and each team's tech lead (spec 023); the other members work through the runs and post there as themselves; an older direct message with a member stays readable (the quick switcher finds it), never deleted.

- A team's channel is its tech lead: a requirement written there (no member mentioned) is answered by that team's lead as in a direct message — the plan (`Plan: …`, who does each part), the spec, the run, reported in the thread; another team's channel gets that team's lead.

- Each channel remembers its own context: besides its last 40 messages, a memory of what happened there (the requests, the specs made, the runs and how they ended, the plans, the open questions; written without a model call), read only in that channel (a thread reads its own, then its channel's; Atlas's and each direct message have their own). `nuclear-builder chat memory <channel> [--thread <t>] [--clear]` shows or clears it.

rows.title: Can: add your own kinds, definitions and dialects without touching the compiler
rows.summary: A project or the community adds a kind as a package (`kinds/<name>/` with TOML, templates and a runtime), brings type definitions of a library in `<project>/defs/`, and a new target is a new dialect: all data, never Rust.
body: - `nuclear kind new <name> -p <platform> -d <dialect>` writes a kind package's skeleton; `nuclear add <folder>` installs it. A package implemented for some dialects ties the project to them (`N0306`).
- `nuclear add <package>` adds any package of the target with its type definitions (`can:packages`).
- `nuclear dialect check <name|path>` validates a dialect's files.

rows.title: Can: use any library of the target (npm, PyPI, pub.dev) through Nuclear
rows.summary: `nuclear add <package>` installs any package of the project's dialect with that technology's package manager, writes it in `config.nuc` and generates its type definitions: its names are then known to the compiler and the editor, and imported where they are used.
body: - `nuclear add lodash` (nestjs, react: npm), `nuclear add humanize` (fastapi: pip), `nuclear add cached_network_image` (flutter: pub). A version: `nuclear add lodash@4.17.21`. Out again: `nuclear remove lodash`.

- The package goes to `dependencies(...)` of `config.nuc`: `lodash = "^4.18.1"`, or `"date-fns@^4.4.0"` when the name is not an identifier. A package written there by hand gets its definitions with `nuclear install`.
- A backend or web project keeps the definitions in its `defs/` folder, with the sources; a mobile app in the shared cache (`build/defs.lock`).

- Then the names are used directly, without `use`: `nanoid(8)` writes `import { nanoid } from 'nanoid'`, `slugify(title)` writes `from slugify import slugify`. A package's default export is one name: `dayjs()`, `lodash.chunk(list, 2)`.
- Look a name up inside the project: `nuclear defs search <text> --dialect <d>`, `nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect <d>`.
- A package the platform already covers (`express` under nestjs, `flask` under fastapi) is added with a word of advice: the `controller` kind already gives the routes.
- Only for the project's dialect: a Python library cannot be used in a project built for TypeScript, nor a Flutter package in a backend.
- Never install a package by hand inside `build/`: it is not in `config.nuc`, and its names stay unknown (`N0106`).

rows.title: Can: traces and metrics to Datadog, New Relic or Grafana (backend)
rows.summary: With `plugins(telemetry = true)` and one connection (`Datadog`, `NewRelic`, `Grafana` or `Otlp`) a backend sends every request and use case as a span and its metrics over OTLP; `@untraced` leaves out a use case, a route or a controller. Done with fastapi; nestjs does not bring the plugin yet.
body: - `config.nuc`: `plugins(telemetry = true)`; `config/project_config.nuc`: `Datadog(apiKey = env("DD_API_KEY"))`, `NewRelic(licenseKey = env("NEW_RELIC_LICENSE_KEY"), region = "eu")`, `Grafana(url = ..., instanceId = ..., token = ...)` or `Otlp(url = "http://localhost:4318")` in `connections`. Keys always from `env(...)`.
- Every one takes `service` (default: the project's name) and `sample` (the share of traces kept, 1 = all).
- No code for the spans: each request and each use case's `exec` (named `component › usecase › Class.exec`); an `Err` marks the span as an error.
- Business metrics: `Metric.count("orders.created", region = r)`, `Metric.record("orders.total", total)`.
- `@untraced` on a use case (no span), on a route (the request starts no trace, e.g. a health check) or on a controller (every route). Without the plugin it does nothing.
- Not yet: nestjs, spans of queries, outgoing HTTP, listeners and agents; `Log` with the trace.

rows.title: Can: real time over WebSockets, by configuration (backend and web)
rows.summary: Real time is configuration: a backend with `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` serves its same controllers over a WebSocket and pushes what it publishes; a web app with a `WebSocket(url)` connection instead of `Http` sends its repositories' calls over it, unchanged, and receives what is pushed as a `Stream<T>`. The same Nuclear for every dialect.
body: - Backend: `plugins(events = true, websocket = true)`, `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` in the `appConfig`'s connections; `~publish("tasks.created", value)` reaches the clients subscribed to `tasks.created`. The app's guards check the upgrade.
- Web: `WebSocket(url = "ws://localhost:8000/ws", headers, timeout, interceptors)` in `connections`; the repositories stay as they are (one line of config switches HTTP to WebSockets).

- What is pushed: a repository method `@on("topic")` (it may use the method's parameters: `@on("chat.${workspace}") events(workspace: string)`) without a body that returns `Stream<T>`; a use case passes it on (`exec() Stream<T>`, no `~`; `nuclear gen usecase <c> <Name> --calls <Repo>.<method>` writes it); a state manager follows it with `listen(stream, (value) => ...)` until its screen leaves.
- The frames (JSON): `{id, method, path, headers, body}` → `{id, status, body}`; `{subscribe}`, `{unsubscribe}`; `{event, data}`.
- `nuclear new <name> -p backend --websocket`, `nuclear new <name> -p web --websocket`.
- The contract says `webSocket`, each controller's `transports` and the `events` the app publishes.
- Tested in the project: `ws = (~appClient().socket("/ws", headers = TOKEN)).value`, `~ws.subscribe(t)`, `~ws.request(...)`, `~ws.next()` (see can:test-the-app).

rows.title: Can: guards on a backend's routes (a header token, no web pages)
rows.summary: A backend checks the headers of every request before its route runs: `Token(value, header)` (401 without it) and `NoOrigin()` (403 for a request from a web page), for the whole app in the `appConfig` or for one controller, over HTTP and over the app's WebSocket. Never a token in the query.
body: - `guards: Guard[] = [NoOrigin(), Token(value = env("TOKEN"), header = "X-Token")]` in the `appConfig`: every route, the contract's routes and the WebSocket's upgrade.
- `@controller("admin", guards = [Token(value = env("ADMIN_TOKEN"))])`: that controller's routes, after the app's guards.
- `Token` reads `Authorization: Bearer <value>` by default; an empty value (an unset variable) refuses everything.
- A guarded app serves no documentation pages; the contract lists the guards with their headers, never a value.
- A project's tests prove them: `app = appClient()`, `expect((~app.get("/x")).status == 401)`, with the test token of `testEnv(TOKEN = "test")` in `config.nuc` (see can:test-the-app).
- `nuclear new <name> -p backend --token <ENV_VAR>` writes them.
- Not yet: users, sessions, a guard kind for checks beyond headers.

rows.title: Can: let a web app on another origin call a backend (CORS)
rows.summary: `origins: string[]` in the backend's `appConfig` lists the web origins whose browsers may call the API (a web app served on another port or host): their requests are answered with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`; any other origin's browser is blocked. The same in every backend dialect.
body: - `origins: string[] = [env("WEB_ORIGIN", "http://localhost:5173")]` in `config/project_config.nuc`, beside `connections`.
- Without `origins`, no browser on another origin can call the API: a web app that reads the backend fails with a CORS error in its console.
- `NoOrigin()` (a guard) does the opposite: it refuses every request from a web page.

rows.title: Can: a web app mounted in a host's page (web)
rows.summary: Every web build also writes `mount(element, host)`: the app mounted in an element of another page (an editor's webview, another site), in a shadow root with its stylesheet, the host's CSS variables as its theme, an in-memory router, and every call through the host's bridge when given.
body: - In `build/app`: `npm run build:embed` → `dist-embed/embed.js`, one ES module with React inside.

rows.title: Can: test a backend as its clients call it (HTTP, its WebSocket, its guards)
rows.summary: A backend's `tests` call the app over HTTP and over its WebSocket with `appClient()`, with the test's connections and the environment of `testEnv(...)` in `config.nuc` (a test token, never a real one); the same Nuclear for every dialect.
body: - `app = appClient()`; `~app.get(path, headers = {...})`, `~app.post(path, body = ..., headers = ...)`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `request(method, path, body, headers)` → `HttpAnswer` (`status`, `body`).

- `~app.socket("/ws", headers = {...})` → `Ok(AppSocket)` or `Err` with 401/403 when a guard refuses the upgrade; `~ws.subscribe(topic)`, `~ws.request(...)`, `~ws.next(seconds = 2)` (a `SocketEvent`: `topic`, `data`; `null` when none), `~ws.close()`.
- `body` and `headers` are always named arguments.
- `testEnv(TASKS_TOKEN = "test-tasks-token")` in `config.nuc`: set before the app is loaded, only for the tests.
- Examples: `tasks_api/test/api_test.nuc`, `nuclear-chat/nuclear_chat/test/api_test.nuc`.

rows.title: Can: the agents do everything the Builder's UI does (nuclear-builder mcp)
rows.summary: Every action of Nuclear Builder's pages is a `nuclear-builder` command and a tool of its MCP server, `nuclear-builder mcp`: an agent reads the slides, writes the specs with their criteria, starts their runs, answers their gates and keeps the teams and the line. The factory gives the server to every agent it runs, beside `nuclear-mcp`; what spends money, destroys or acts in the user's name waits for the user.
body: - In the chat: `read docs/slides.pdf and write all the specs from those slides, then write the code through the Builder` — the member calls `project_read` (a PDF with pdftotext, a .pptx, markdown), `spec_new` with the acceptance criteria (refused without them: it asks), then `run_start` for each spec; each run is told in its thread.

- 57 tools (the skills too: `skills_list`, `skills_show`, `skills_clone`, `skills_create`, `skills_update`, `skills_delete`, `team_skills_set`; `models_list`, `agents_list`): specs (`spec_new`, `spec_list`, `spec_show`, `spec_update` (the whole spec, the user approves), `spec_draft`, `spec_accept`, `spec_discard`, `spec_move`, `spec_migrate`, `spec_delete`), runs (`run_start`, `runs`, `run_file`, `run_journal`, `run_answer`, `run_resume`, `run_retry`, `run_restart`, `run_stop`), the reports (`metrics`), QA's plan (`checks`, `check_switch`, `check_add`, `check_mark`), teams (`team_*`: the new-team wizard's `team_create`, `team_suggest`, `team_name_suggest`, `team_runnable`, `team_member_add|remove|update`), the line (`line_show`, `line_set`), `ci_export`, `connections_check`, `project_read`, `vault_list`, `agents_list` (the agents a conversation can choose on this machine).

- In a workspace (a workspace's own channel): its specs and runs are its apps'. `spec_new` takes `app`, the app the spec is for, and is refused without one (it lists the apps). The tools of a spec or a run work in the app that holds it. `spec_list` and `runs` say each one's app. A spec at the workspace's root is never run there.

- Money: only work paid by use (kind `api`) is asked; a tool never confirms it: it answers `waiting: spending` and the run waits for the user's two confirmations (the editor's two questions, or two in the chat); an agent's subscription is not asked; force confirmation asks everything.

- The user's: deleting a spec or a team, a restart from scratch, the delivery gate (a commit and a pull request in the user's name), the line's gates, commands and forceConfirm, replacing a CI file answer `needsUser`; the chat asks the user and applies it on a yes. Merging is never a tool; an API key is kept only by the user. `run_retry` that takes files back also needs the user's yes (`confirm`).

- Every agent gets it: Claude Code (`--mcp-config`, `mcp__nuclear_builder`), OpenCode (its `mcp` table), Codex (`-c mcp_servers.nuclear_builder.*`), Gemini CLI (its settings), Cursor (a plugin of the run, `--plugin-dir`), Grok Build (the run's own `GROK_HOME`), an API model's loop (a second MCP client).
- Your own agent: `claude mcp add nuclear_builder -- nuclear-builder mcp --root <project>`.

rows.title: Can: read what the factory spent and made (nuclear-builder metrics, the Reports page)
rows.summary: Every Builder step and Nuclear Chat answer is a line of the factory's ledger (`~/.config/nuclearlang/factory/ledger/`, every project, on the machine only): who, where, the tokens and money the provider reported, the time, the lines added and removed, the result. `nuclear-builder metrics` and the MCP tool `metrics` read it as a bill and Jira-like reports; VS Code's *Reports* tool (Ctrl+Alt+K) draws them.
body: - The views: `bill` (tokens in and out, USD, local against paid, by period, provider and model, team, member, project; the budget each run used), `throughput` (specs delivered, velocity by team), `cycle` (cycle time and time per station), `burndown`, `flow` (cumulative flow), `waiting` (the gates open now and how long), `quality` (failures, retries, first-try pass rate per station), `people` (each member's steps, answers, lines, passes, fails, tokens, money), `indicators` (cost per delivered spec, tokens per useful line, the local share).

- `nuclear-builder metrics [--project <name|dir>] [--team <id>] [--member <id>] [--from YYYY-MM-DD] [--to YYYY-MM-DD] [--by day|week] [--view <view>] --json`; the MCP tool takes `since` and `until` for the dates.
- Measured at the source, never estimated: Claude Code's usage, OpenCode's steps, Codex's and Gemini CLI's turns, the APIs' usage; a provider that reports none is counted as not reported.
- A member's numbers are also in their panel's Summary on *Your software company*; the runs of before are copied into the ledger once, with what their files had.

rows.title: Can: call the helpers of lodash with no import (chunk, uniqBy, partition, camelCase, get, merge...)
rows.summary: Nuclear has 117 helpers over lists, maps, texts, numbers and functions (the functions of lodash that serve Nuclear), called with no `use` in every dialect; the transpiler writes into the output only the helpers a program calls.
body: - Lists: `chunk(xs, 2)`, `compact`, `difference`, `intersection`, `union`, `xor` (and their `By` / `With` forms), `uniqBy(users, (u) => u.name)`, `dropWhile`, `takeRight`, `fill`, `nth`, `pull`, `remove`, `sortedIndex`, `zip`, `unzip`, `zipWith`, `zipObject`.
- Collections: `countBy`, `keyBy`, `partition`, `reject`, `flatMap`, `reduceRight`, `orderBy(xs, keys, descending)`, `sample`, `shuffle`.
- Numbers: `mean`, `meanBy`, `sumBy`, `maxBy`, `minBy`, `roundTo(n, 2)`, `floorTo`, `ceilTo`, `inRange`, `randomInt`, `range(0, 20, 5)`, `rangeRight`.

- Texts: `camelCase`, `kebabCase`, `snakeCase`, `startCase`, `lowerCase`, `upperCase`, `capitalize`, `upperFirst`, `lowerFirst`, `words`, `truncate`, `pad`, `escape`, `unescape`, `escapeRegExp`, `trimChars`.

- Maps and data: `pick`, `omit`, `pickBy`, `omitBy`, `mapValues`, `mapKeys`, `invert`, `defaults`, `findKey`, `toPairs`, `fromPairs`, `get(data, "a.b[0]")`, `set`, `has`, `unset`, `cloneDeep`, `merge`.
- Functions: `once`, `memoize`, `after`, `before`, `negate`, `flip`, `partial`, `curry`, `flow`, `flowRight`, `times`, `attempt`, `identity`, `constant`, `uniqueIds`.
- They are functions, never members: what a base type already has stays its member (`xs.map(f)`, `xs.unique()`, `xs.groupBy(key)`, `s.trim()`), and no helper repeats it.
- An iteratee is a lambda, and its parameters take their types from the helper. `zip`, `partition` and `toPairs` give `Pair<A, B>` (`first`, `second`): Nuclear has no tuples.

- A name is a helper only where nothing nearer defines it: a local, a member, a declaration of the project or a name imported with `use` is the program's own. A helper wins over a function a target has under the same name.
- Each helper has its own row (`lib:helper-<name>`) with its signature and the cases its tests state. Every signature: `nuclear help helpers`.

rows.title: Can: prove that the same Nuclear runs the same in every dialect (the test sets of the language and the backend)
rows.summary: Nuclear is tested by running the same programs in TypeScript, Dart and Python and comparing what they print, with no warning of each target's checker allowed; a backend is tested on real databases in Docker with both dialects answering the same bytes.
body: - **The conformance programs** (`nuclearlang/examples/conformance`, 26): one per feature, each case a labelled line. Operators (arithmetic, comparison, logic, bits, assignment, null, conditional); `if`, `match`, loops; functions, lambdas and closures; modules, inheritance, enums, generics; `try`, `Result`; `~` and generators; texts, lists, maps, scope; texts as data (no `$&`, no `\1`); the helpers. Run: `DIR=examples/conformance nuclearlang/tools/stdlib-check.sh`.

- **The semantics programs** (`examples/semantics`): one rule a target once broke each (a lambda made in a loop, `==` of two lists, a decimal printed with its `.0`). **The standard library programs** (`examples/stdlib`): one per area.
- **The helpers' cases** (`nuclear-synapsis-framework/lodash/check.sh`): 226 cases from lodash's own tests, run twice: with the helpers as a project's files, and brought by the compiler.

- **The database check** (`platforms/backend/checks/database-check`, Docker): one project built with `fastapi` and `nestjs` on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB: 13 migration scenarios through `nuclear migrate` (add, change, rename and drop columns, foreign keys, a failure under each transaction mode, `--fake`, `--to`, a history of before 0.93 converted); the schemas of the two dialects must be the same after every step, 57 HTTP answers that must be the same bytes (CRUD, relations, pages, a transaction that rolls back, 400 / 404 / 409 with their bodies), and its unit tests. Also there: a value of another JSON type refused for each type, the milliseconds of a `DateTime` read back, a model built in code that breaks its rule, and the tables `createTables` makes against the first migration's. And: renames with `make --rename` (the rows and the foreign key follow), a text of 100000 and of 5000000 characters, what the database refuses for integrity answered 409.
- **The benchmarks** (`eval/thesis/bench`, 8): the generated code against an expert's in each target (n-body, binary trees, fannkuch, a collections pipeline, texts, calls, primes, word frequencies).
- Each target's own checker runs with no warning allowed: `tsc --strict` with no unused name, `dart analyze --fatal-warnings`, pyright.
- Every change to the transpiler, a dialect or the library runs them all first (ADR-platform-0014); the CI runs them (`language`, `platform-backend`).
- The programs are in the base as examples: `example:conformance/<name>`, `example:semantics/<name>`, `example:bench/<name>`, each with what it prints.

rows.title: Can: one body for every error and one OpenAPI document, whatever the dialect (backend)
rows.summary: Every error of a backend answers `{status, message}`, and an invalid body or parameter adds `errors`, one reason per field (`field`, `rule`, `message`); `GET /openapi.json` answers the document written from the project. The same in `fastapi` and `nestjs`.
body: - An error: `{ "status": 404, "message": "no task 9" }`. The message is the `Err`'s (`NotFound("no task 9")`), `not found` for a route that does not exist, `error` for what nothing handled (a 500 never says why).

- An invalid body or parameter: 400, `message` `invalid`, and `errors`: one reason per field, in the order of the fields' names: `{ "field": "priority", "rule": "max", "message": "priority must be at most 3" }`.

- What the database refuses for integrity: 409 `{ "status": 409, "message": "conflict" }` on every database and in every dialect (a repeated unique value, a foreign key that points at no row, a row removed while others point to it, a null in a required column, a text longer than its column); never the database's own text. A use case that checks first answers its own `Err(Conflict("..."))` message.

- `rule` is the validation's name in Nuclear: `required`, `type`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `min`, `max`, `pattern`, `email`, `url`, `json` (the body is not JSON), `invalid`. A field that breaks several names the first of that list. `field` is a path (`items.0.name`).
- Each runtime converts what its framework reports into that body, so a client never knows the dialect.
- `GET /openapi.json` and `GET /.nuclear/openapi.json`: the OpenAPI 3.1 document the transpiler writes from the contract; its `Error` schema is this body.
- A client that read `detail` or `statusCode` (before 0.91) reads `message` and `status`.
